newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian T-bills open firmer amid overseas buying.
newsitem.headline: Canadian T-bills open firmer amid overseas buying.

text.p: Canadian T-bills opened mostly firmer on Friday, despite strong U.S. GDP data, as buying by dealers and overseas accounts helped send prices higher, analysts said.

"For the most part people are staying on the sidelines, taking profits where ever they can and waiting for the market to back up again. There's been some overseas buying, that also is also likely shortcovering. Most of it, really since the tender, has been a market dominated by the street," said Walter Posiewko, a money market trader with Royal Bank Investment Management.
Canada's three-month when-issued T-bill firmed to yield 3.28 percent from 3.29 percent at the close of trading on Thurday.

Most North American fixed-income markets were weaker on Friday after the U.S. Labor Department reported that the economy added 316,000 jobs in July and the jobless rate stood at 4.8 percent. Economists had forecast non-farm payrolls growth of 193,000 and a jobless rate of 4.9 percent.
Dealers said the Canadian money market was benefiting from the momentum it had gained since Tuesday's weekly T-bill tender came in well bid.
In other prices, the six-month when-issued T-bill firmed to yield 3.56 percent from 3.57 percent on Thursday. The one-year when-issued T-bill firmed to yield 4.07 percent from 4.09 percent.

The call loan or overnight lending rate traded at 3.25 percent, in the center of the Bank of Canada's 3.0-3.5 percent target range. The central bank on Thursday intervened on the money market three times with specials after the call loan rate traded at the top of the band.
